record.paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
record.context_brief: Coulombic origin of molecular density topology
record.original_question: How do Coulombic interactions between nuclei and electrons determine the topology of the molecular one-electron density so that topological atoms arise naturally? In particular, what mathematical mechanism makes nuclear attractors the usual attractors of the density-gradient field in Coulombic molecular systems, whereas replacing Coulomb interactions by harmonic interactions can produce a different density topology?

evidence.quote: This reasoning was implicitly confirmed when we tried to apply the QTAIM analysis to a hypothetical model of molecule where the coulombic interactions between electrons and nuclei were replaced by the harmonic potential, i.e. the Hookean model of molecule [28].

The results of the analysis on the Hookean H2+ demonstrated that instead of two attractors in on each of the nuclei, a single attractor emerges in the middle of the nuclei [28]. Evidently, the fact that the attractors of in the coulombic systems are usually revealed only on the nuclei is not something trivial and is tied intrinsically to the nature of the interaction of nuclei and electrons. Accordingly, the naturalness problem may be cast in a more concrete language: How the coulombic interactions between nuclei and electrons dictate the topology of the one-electron density in a way that the concept of the topological atom arises naturally?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let a molecular system consist of $M$ fixed nuclei at positions $\{R_A\}_{A=1}^M$ with charges $\{Z_A\}$ and $N$ electrons described by an antisymmetric ground-state wavefunction $\Psi$ of the Hamiltonian
$$ H = -\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_i^2 + V_{ne} + V_{ee}, $$
yielding the one-electron density
$$ \rho(r) = N \int |\Psi(r,r_2,\dots,r_N)|^2\, dr_2\cdots dr_N. $$
The gradient vector field $\nabla\rho$ partitions $\mathbb{R}^3$ into basins whose attractors (local maxima of $\rho$) define the topological atoms of the Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules.

Empirically, when the electron–nucleus and electron–electron interactions are Coulombic,
$$ V_{ne}(r) = -\sum_{A,i}\frac{Z_A}{|r_i - R_A|}, \qquad V_{ee} = \sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{|r_i-r_j|}, $$
every attractor of $\nabla\rho$ coincides with a nuclear position (modulo rare non-nuclear attractors). In contrast, when these interactions are replaced by harmonic (Hookean) potentials, e.g. for a two-nucleus one-electron system
$$ V_{ne}^{H}(r) = \tfrac{1}{2}k\big(|r-R_1|^2 + |r-R_2|^2\big), $$
a single attractor of $\rho$ emerges at the midpoint of the nuclei rather than two attractors at the nuclei.

Problem. Provide a rigorous mathematical mechanism, derived from the structure of the many-body Schrödinger equation, that explains why for Coulombic electron–nucleus interactions the attractors of the one-electron density gradient field are generically located at the nuclear positions, and that simultaneously accounts for the failure of this property when the Coulomb potential is replaced by a harmonic potential. In particular, identify the precise feature of the $1/|r-R_A|$ singularity (for instance via Kato's cusp condition or related local analysis of $\rho$ near nuclei) that forces $R_A$ to be a local maximum of $\rho$, and characterize the class of electron–nucleus interaction potentials for which the topological atoms of QTAIM coincide with the nuclei.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of why Coulombic interactions force the attractors of the one-electron density to lie on nuclei, while harmonic (Hookean) interactions do not, is discussed as a foundational open problem in the QTAIM literature. While Kato's cusp condition guarantees that $\rho$ has local maxima at nuclei in Coulombic systems, a complete mathematical characterization of the interaction potentials for which the topological atoms coincide with nuclei does not appear to have been established. Recent QTAIM literature continues to treat the Hookean counterexample as motivation for extending QTAIM beyond Coulombic systems, without providing a definitive resolution.

status_evidence.title: What is an Atom in a Molecule
status_evidence.snippet: Hookean molecules are model systems where some Coulombic interactions are replaced by harmonic potentials; QTAIM applied to them yields AIM structures not matching chemical intuition.
status_evidence.claim: Hookean models give different density topology, motivating the open question of how Coulombic interactions dictate QTAIM topology.

status_evidence.title: On Quantum Chemical Topology
status_evidence.snippet: Most QTAIM ingredients are not sensitive to the explicit form of the potential, but Coulombic interactions are assumed in defining basin energies.
status_evidence.claim: The mathematical role of Coulombic interactions in producing the standard QTAIM topology remains an active subject of investigation.
